scope: Independent ProjectX architecture decision package, grounded in product discovery, not inferred from SevenRooms internals.

decisions.title: Deployment topology and hosting
decisions.question: Which independently designed deployment and hosting model should ProjectX use for the first production milestone?

options.description: Managed modular monolith: one backend deployable, separately served web client and managed supporting services.
options.pros: Few operational boundaries, simple transactions and incremental tasks.
options.cons: The backend must maintain clear module boundaries; deploy cadence is shared.
options.bestWhen: First production release with a small team.

options.description: Hybrid: core modular backend plus independently deployed integrations and background workers.
options.pros: Isolates optional external work.
options.cons: More deployment and tracing surfaces from day one.
options.bestWhen: Integrations already demand independent scale or ownership.

options.description: Microservices per major domain on managed infrastructure.
options.pros: Independent scaling and team ownership.
options.cons: Distributed transactions, operations and testing cost rise sharply.
options.bestWhen: Multiple domain teams and proven scale demand.

options.description: Self-hosted/on-premises application with owner-managed infrastructure.
options.pros: Direct infrastructure control.
options.cons: Highest patching, recovery and monitoring burden.
options.bestWhen: Contractual hosting restrictions require it.

recommendedDefault.reason: The visible flows have strong cross-module transactions and no measured need for distributed deployment. Hosting provider remains a separate selection after requirements and cost approval.

decisions.rationale: Deployment model and hosting account shape operating cost, recovery, and how many moving parts every small task must verify.
evidence: 16 mapped product modules; 144 screens; reservation, availability and client journeys cross module boundaries.
No evidence of reference deployment topology or cloud provider.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: Frontend framework and runtime
decisions.question: Which frontend/backend/runtime and repository combination should be the starting implementation contract?

options.description: React + TypeScript web client, Node.js LTS + Fastify backend, one workspace monorepo.
options.pros: Shared language/types and explicit API boundary; small task slices.
options.cons: Requires discipline to keep shared types and modules decoupled.
options.bestWhen: A compact team wants typed end-to-end delivery.

options.description: Next.js + TypeScript web application, Node.js LTS + NestJS modular backend, monorepo.
options.pros: Integrated web workflow and strong backend conventions.
options.cons: More framework conventions and runtime surface.
options.bestWhen: Team favors framework structure and server rendering.

options.description: React + TypeScript web client, Python + FastAPI backend, monorepo.
options.pros: Clear frontend/backend separation and mature Python ecosystem.
options.cons: Two-language contract generation and tooling.
options.bestWhen: Python expertise or analytical workloads dominate.

options.description: React + TypeScript web client, Java + Spring backend, separate repositories.
options.pros: Mature backend tooling and independent release governance.
options.cons: Higher setup and cross-repo contract coordination cost.
options.bestWhen: Large organization with established JVM operations.

recommendedDefault.reason: Form-heavy web UI and many bounded tasks benefit from an explicit typed client/API seam and one reviewable repository; no stack is inferred from SevenRooms.

decisions.rationale: The stack determines developer workflow, shared contracts, deployment toolchain and the cost of changing frameworks later.
evidence: 144 screens with editable forms, calendar, floorplan and nested panels; 16 modules intended as small independently verifiable tasks.
No reference framework, language or repository structure is observable.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: Primary database and tenant storage
decisions.question: What data store and account/organization/venue isolation model should ProjectX enforce?

options.description: PostgreSQL shared schema with explicit organization/venue scope and database row-level policies plus application authorization.
options.pros: Strong relational transactions and layered isolation at moderate cost.
options.cons: Policy context and cross-venue reporting require disciplined testing.
options.bestWhen: Multi-venue SaaS with controlled sharing.

options.description: PostgreSQL schema per organization, venue keys inside each schema.
options.pros: Coarse organization boundary.
options.cons: Migrations and pooled connections multiply with tenant count.
options.bestWhen: Few large organizations need schema-level separation.

options.description: PostgreSQL database per organization or venue.
options.pros: Strong physical separation and tailored recovery.
options.cons: Cost and migration/analytics operations grow substantially.
options.bestWhen: Isolation contracts require dedicated data stores.

options.description: Managed document store with application-enforced tenant predicates.
options.pros: Flexible documents and rapid schema evolution.
options.cons: Cross-entity transactions and omission of a scope filter become harder to control.
options.bestWhen: Data relationships prove document-oriented and isolation requirements allow it.

recommendedDefault.reason: Observed relationships and reservation concurrency call for transactions and explicit scoped queries. The hierarchy and client-sharing rules must be confirmed before finalizing keys.

decisions.rationale: Tenant hierarchy and isolation determine every data key, authorization query, backup scope and the consequences of an access bug.
evidence: Venue selector; user form mentions the same access at other venues; venue-scoped routes; reservation links to client, shift, area and table.
The exact account→organization→venue hierarchy and cross-venue sharing semantics are UNKNOWN.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: Authentication and session strategy
decisions.question: How should users authenticate, hold sessions, and receive venue-scoped privileges?

options.description: Managed OIDC identity provider with secure server-managed sessions; internal venue-scoped RBAC plus explicit permission checks.
options.pros: Reduces credential storage burden and supports MFA; app keeps object authorization.
options.cons: Provider cost and migration/availability dependency.
options.bestWhen: A secure first release without running a credential service.

options.description: First-party credential and MFA service with server sessions plus scoped RBAC.
options.pros: Maximum control over sign-in.
options.cons: Highest credential recovery, abuse and security operations burden.
options.bestWhen: Strong in-house identity expertise and special constraints.

options.description: Enterprise SSO only with externally asserted roles and local venue grants.
options.pros: Central organization identity.
options.cons: Excludes users without supported enterprise IdP; mapping claims needs care.
options.bestWhen: Only enterprise customers are in scope.

options.description: External identity provider and stateless access tokens with scoped RBAC/ABAC checks.
options.pros: Good for multiple clients and APIs.
options.cons: Refresh/revocation and browser token storage require care.
options.bestWhen: Several trusted client types require token exchange.

recommendedDefault.reason: It separates identity proofing from app-owned, per-object and per-venue authorization and avoids storing passwords in the first milestone.

decisions.rationale: The account exposes guest PII, payment-related controls and cross-venue access; credential ownership and permission scope are security boundaries.
evidence: User Accounts displays access levels, granular permissions, MFA option and multi-venue assignment; only one account role was observed.
Alternate-role authorization and actual sign-in/session semantics remain UNKNOWN.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: API contract model
decisions.question: Which API style and validation/contract authority should connect the web client and domain modules?

options.description: Versioned REST resources with OpenAPI as reviewed contract, generated client types and server runtime validation.
options.pros: Clear HTTP semantics and diffable contracts for small tasks.
options.cons: Some complex composed reads need dedicated projections.
options.bestWhen: Standard CRUD and workflow commands dominate.

options.description: GraphQL schema with typed operations and runtime input validation.
options.pros: Flexible composite reads.
options.cons: Field-level authorization/cost limits and caching are more complex.
options.bestWhen: Many distinct clients need independently selected data.

options.description: Typed RPC over HTTP with schema-owned client/server contracts.
options.pros: Fast type-safe iteration in one repository.
options.cons: Public integration and versioning require extra discipline.
options.bestWhen: Only controlled first-party clients exist.

options.description: Hybrid REST commands plus GraphQL read layer and shared schema definitions.
options.pros: Optimizes different read/write shapes.
options.cons: Two contract models from the start.
options.bestWhen: Measured composite read needs justify it.

recommendedDefault.reason: It offers explicit versioned, testable boundaries and reduces the chance that one screen change forces broad module edits.

decisions.rationale: Contract shape controls independent task ownership, integration verification and future client compatibility.
evidence: Many form fields, sortable lists, calendars and state changes; no reference API implementation or schema is evidenced.
Roadmap requires focused API contract tests for each module.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: Background jobs and events
decisions.question: When and how should background jobs and events be implemented?

recommendedDefault.proposal: No queue or event broker chosen before a workflow requires asynchronous work. Design outbox/worker and retry contract before first irreversible delivery.

decisions.rationale: No queue or event broker chosen before a workflow requires asynchronous work. Design outbox/worker and retry contract before first irreversible delivery.
evidence: Potential communication, export and import work is visible; delivery execution unobserved.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: Cache strategy
decisions.question: When and how should cache strategy be implemented?

recommendedDefault.proposal: No shared cache until measured reads justify it; any future cache must be scoped by tenant/venue and invalidated on writes.

decisions.rationale: No shared cache until measured reads justify it; any future cache must be scoped by tenant/venue and invalidated on writes.
evidence: Availability is time-sensitive and correctness is more important than speculative caching.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.

decisions.title: Audit and event history
decisions.question: When and how should audit and event history be implemented?

recommendedDefault.proposal: Append-only actor/venue/object/action audit metadata for security and lifecycle changes; segregate from editable comments and minimize PII.

decisions.rationale: Append-only actor/venue/object/action audit metadata for security and lifecycle changes; segregate from editable comments and minimize PII.
evidence: Reservation detail showed activity events and user/permission settings are visible.

decisions.title: Backup and recovery objectives
decisions.question: What production recovery target and environment/CI spending envelope should guide infrastructure design?

options.description: Pilot: daily backups, target RPO 24 hours/RTO 24 hours; development and production plus ephemeral CI.
options.pros: Lowest recurring cost.
options.cons: Large potential data-loss/service interruption window.
options.bestWhen: Disposable pilot with low operational dependence.

options.description: Operational baseline: target RPO 1 hour/RTO 4 hours; separate dev, staging, production and restore drills.
options.pros: Balanced service continuity and repeatable release checks.
options.cons: Higher managed backup/staging cost.
options.bestWhen: Restaurant operations depend on the app during service.

options.description: High availability: target RPO 5 minutes/RTO 1 hour with failover and frequent restore rehearsals.
options.pros: Short disruption and data loss.
options.cons: Significantly higher cost and operational complexity.
options.bestWhen: Contractual uptime commitments justify it.

options.description: Owner-defined custom targets and environment constraints.
options.pros: Fits existing hosting contracts or unusual operations.
options.cons: Requires explicit numbers and operational ownership before design.
options.bestWhen: There are binding organizational requirements.

recommendedDefault.reason: Live reservations warrant a recoverable staging-to-production process, while no evidence justifies high-availability infrastructure yet. Targets are recommendations, not guarantees.

decisions.rationale: Reservation operations can affect active service; recovery expectations determine backup frequency, restore rehearsal and staging cost.
evidence: The product handles reservations, clients and operational shift settings, but no traffic, budget, RPO, RTO or regulatory retention target is documented.
Production write behavior has not been tested.
decisions.notes: Future test/data may refine implementation; not approved.
